note: The pipeline blocks of the last step: from the 3D models and the headset's sensors to the picture in the lenses. Short labels only: the full text and what to say is plans/pipeline.md. 'when' is once (setup), session (once per Enter VR) or frame (every frame). 'on' is where a stage runs; style B places it there and style D puts the frame stages on the loop.

stages.title: 0 · Setup (once)
lines: Developer Mode, adb over USB-C or Wi-Fi
the headset's localhost:8798 is the laptop

stages.title: 1 · Load the scene
lines: page, three.js, steps, 3D models (~11 MB)
meshes copied once into GPU memory

stages.title: 2 · Enter VR
lines: an immersive session, origin on the floor
the headset takes over the displays

stages.title: 3 · Track
lines: cameras + motion sensor → head pose (6DoF)
controllers: pose, buttons, stick

stages.title: 4 · Update (CPU)
lines: pose predicted for when the frame shows
our code: buttons → steps, timelines, fades

stages.title: 5 · Render twice (GPU)
lines: one camera per eye, as far apart as your eyes
both eyes drawn into one image

stages.title: 6 · Show
lines: re-aimed to the newest pose, pre-warped for the lens
two displays, two lenses: your brain sees depth

blend.title: Inside a .blend file (Z-Anatomy.blend)
lines: BLENDER-v292   Blender 2.92, 64-bit, little-endian
then 100,172 blocks: pieces of Blender's memory,
each: code · size · old address · type · count
OB "Nasal bone.r"   an object: place, parent
.data  → ME   a mesh: counts, array addresses
.mvert → DATA 148 vertices (x, y, z)
.mpoly → DATA 292 faces: first corner, count
.mloop → DATA 876 corners: vertex, edge
.medge → DATA 438 edges
.mat   → MA   material "Bone"
DNA1   the catalogue: every struct's fields
Whole file: 2,650 OB, 1,565 ME, 32 MA;
98% of the bytes are DATA arrays.
glTF keeps vertices, normals, triangles.
No edges: the GPU only draws triangles.

load.note: Steps pipeline-load and pipeline-site. Grounded 2026-11-17 in the vendored code: GLTFLoader.js:298-301 fetches each file as an arraybuffer, :424-447 parses glTF; three.js draws through a webgl2 context (gl.bufferData) and gets head pose and eye views from WebXR (requestReferenceSpace, XRWebGLBinding). WebXR loads no models. The logo is files/icon.svg of the three.js repo (MIT). The robot (2026-11-17): three.js with arms; load step: the GLTFLoader arm grabs the file blocks, the WebGL arm pushes them into the GPU; frame step: pose from WebXR, update, draw x2 into the GPU, the frame to the displays. Labels are one-line names stuck to their part (2026-11-17): each arm, its claw and its name share a colour, and the names of what is working light up; the explanation is the step text, the sources are behind X / S. OpenXR (2026-11-17, Dominic): a slab under the WebXR block (the pose rises through it) and a gate on the conveyor (the frame passes it); step pipeline-openxr shows three apps on one OpenXR bar. Evidence: plans/pipeline.md, 'Under WebXR: OpenXR'. Logos (2026-11-17): logos/webxr.svg is media/logo/webxr-logo.svg of immersive-web/webxr-samples (MIT); logos/openxr.svg is the OpenXR logo from khronos.org/assets/images/api_logos/openxr.svg (OpenXR and its logo are trademarks of The Khronos Group, shown unaltered to name the standard). They replace the WebXR and OpenXR name pills. The displays and lenses sit inside a small see-through copy of the headset (headset.glb), one device at the end of the conveyor; the OpenXR slab and gate are joined by one teal rail, the gate is the headset's door (frames in, poses out), and poses ride the rail up to WebXR. On the OpenXR board three.js lines up with Unity/Unreal (what you write in) and WebXR, inside the browser, with their OpenXR plug-in (what talks to OpenXR); the browser is the program OpenXR actually sees.
